title: Opinion: Archyield Limited v Network Rail Infrastructure Limited
text:
[2024] LTS 6

Lands Tribunal for Scotland

OPINION

Archyield Limited (Applicant) against Network Rail Infrastructure Limited (Respondent)

Application for determination of a question of disputed compensation

The Millennium Hotel, 40 George Square, Glasgow, G2 1DS

Introduction

[1] The applicant was, until 2017, tenant of The Millennium Hotel, 40 George Square, Glasgow in terms of the lease among British Railways Board, British Transport Hotels Limited and the applicant dated 5 and 9 January 1984 and recorded in the Division of the General Register of Sasines for the County of the Barony of Glasgow on 27 January 1984. The term of the lease is for 125 years until 9 January 2109. The lease was registered in the Title Sheet for the subjects under Title Number GLA156586. The applicant seeks an order for payment of statutory compensation following the promulgation under the Transport and Works (Scotland) Act 2007 of the Network Rail (Glasgow Queen Street Station) Order 2017. That order was made to facilitate work required for the redevelopment of Queen Street railway station and entailed, amongst other works, the acquisition by the respondent and subsequent demolition of the 1970s extension to the original hotel building.

[2] The applicant applied to the respondent for payment of compensation in relation to the compulsory purchase of the tenant’s interest in the lease in so far as comprising the demolished part of the hotel. Although interim compensation has been paid, parties have been unable to agree on the full amount of compensation due. The respondent contends the applicant’s valuation of its loss is overstated in respect that the applicant was in breach of its repairing obligations under the lease. Parties disagree as to the proper construction of the lease, specifically in respect of the extent of the applicant’s repairing obligation in terms of Clause (THIRD). Parties agree, however, that resolution of the disagreement as to the correct interpretation of the extent of the applicant’s repairing obligation in terms of the lease will have a material effect on the basis and value of the compensation due to the applicant. They accordingly seek a preliminary determination from the Tribunal as to the correct interpretation of Clause (THIRD).

[3] The matter called before the Tribunal at a diet of debate on 13 December 2023. Mr Burnet KC appeared for the applicant. Mr Manson, advocate appeared for the respondent. We are grateful to both counsel for their clear and succinct oral and written submissions.

The lease

[4] Clause (THIRD) of the lease provides, inter alia , as follows:

“The Tenants [Applicant] hereby accept the premises in their present condition as suitable for the purpose for which they are let and undertake to uphold, maintain and keep the premises in good and tenantable order and condition at all times during the currency of this Lease which obligation shall include the maintenance of the premises wind and watertight and the upholding of the water supply and drainage both within and without the premises all to the reasonable satisfaction of the Landlord [Respondent], provided however that the Tenants [Applicant] will not be obliged to maintain the premises in any better condition than they are at the date hereof, as such condition shall be evidenced by a Schedule of Condition in respect of the premises to be agreed by the parties or, failing agreement, to be settled by arbitration in terms of Clause THIRTY FIRST hereof …”

[5] The applicant contends that, properly construed, Clause (THIRD) requires the tenant only to maintain the premises in the condition they were in at the outset of the lease and avers that at the commencement of the lease the premises were not in a good state of repair. The respondent contends that the standard to which the premises are to be maintained is the objective one of “good and tenantable order and condition”.

Principles of construction

[6] As is invariably the case in such disputes, there was agreement as to the applicable rules of construction but disagreement as to how those principles should be applied to the particular provisions of the lease. As Mr Manson dryly observes in his note of argument, the weight which parties commend should be given to matters of context as opposed to language and vice versa is often dictated by the outcome they are concerned to secure. We were referred variously to Napier v Ferrier (1847) SC 1354; McCall’s Entertainments (Ayr) Ltd v South Ayrshire Council (No 2) 1998 SLT 1421; @SIPP Pension Trustees v Insight Travel Services 2016 SC 243 per Lady Smith at [17] and [43] ‑ [44]; Arnold v Britton [2015] AC 1619 per Lord Neuberger at [14] ‑ [23] and Lord Hodge at [76] ‑ [77]; Dem‑Master Demolition Limited v Healthcare Environmental Services Limited [2017] CSOH 14; Wood v Capita Insurance Services Limited [2017] 2 WLR 1095 per Lord Hodge at [10] ‑ [14]; Scanmudring AS v James Fisher MFE Ltd 2019 SLT 295 per the Lord President at [32]; and Lord Menzies at [63]; and Lagan Construction Group Limited (in administration) v Scot Roads Partnership Project Limited & another [2023] CSIH 28 per the Lord President at [10].

[7] The task for the court when interpreting a commercial lease is a unitary exercise. It is to determine objectively what a reasonable person with all the background knowledge available to both parties at the time of contracting would have understood the parties to have meant by the words they have used. The meaning of a clause in a lease has to be assessed in the light of: (i) the natural and ordinary meaning of the clause, (ii) any other relevant provision of the lease, (iii) the overall purpose of the clause and the lease (iv) the facts and circumstances known or assumed by the parties at the time that the document was executed, and (v) commercial common sense, but (vi) disregarding subjective evidence of any party’s intentions. Commercial common sense should not be invoked to undervalue the importance of the language used by parties in the contractual provision being construed. While poor drafting makes it easier to depart from the natural meaning and clear drafting makes it more difficult to do so, the court is not thereby justified in embarking on an exercise of searching for or constructing drafting infelicities so as to facilitate such departure. Commercial common sense is only relevant to how matters would have been perceived at the time of contracting and is not to be invoked retrospectively. Although commercial common sense is very important, the court should be slow to reject the natural meaning of a provision as correct simply because it seems to be an imprudent term for one of the parties to have agreed, the purpose of interpretation being not to identify what the court thinks that parties ought to have agreed but what they have in fact agreed. The “internal context” of the contract at issue should be considered in seeking to construe a particular term. The court should therefore be concerned to read the contract as a whole in a coherent and consistent way with the result that terms complement rather than contradict one another.

[8] In the context of commercial leases, there is a difference between an obligation to put a premises into repair and an obligation to keep premises in repair. An obligation to keep premises in repair throughout the lease usually implies an understanding of the parties that the premises were in repair when the lease commenced. If that is not the case. and the tenant is to put the premises into repair, that is contrary to the usual understanding, and requires a clear expression of an obligation being placed on the tenant to put the premises into repair: Napier v Ferrier (1847) SC 1354. An implication that premises are in repair at the commencement of a lease can be confirmed or displaced by the express terms of the lease.

Submissions for the applicant

[9] Senior counsel adopted his note of argument. The effect of Clause (THIRD) of the lease in the current case is substantially the same as the Dem‑Master Demolition Limited v Healthcare Environmental Services Limited [2017] CSOH 14 in which the relevant clause provided:

“The Tenants

accept the Premises as being in such condition as shown on the attached Photographic Schedule and in all respects fit for the Tenants’ purposes and
shall at their sole expense and, to the reasonable satisfaction of the Landlords, repair and maintain and renew (and, if necessary for the purposes of maintenance and repair, to replace and rebuild) and decorate and keep the Premises […] in like condition as is evidenced on the said Photographic Schedule and in a clean and tidy condition, clear of all rubbish, for the Duration, […]”

[10] Lady Wolffe found (at paras [217] to [220]) that the actual state of the premises at the outset, as was to be shown in a photographic schedule, was the measure of the parties' obligations. Properly construed, the standard of the premises, as accepted and to which they were to be repaired or kept for the duration of the lease, was assessed by reference to their actual state at the material time, as evidenced by the photographic schedule rather than a notional or objective standard. The omission of the preparation of the expected photographic schedule at the material time had, at most, evidential consequences and did not affect the determination of the proper construction of the clause.

[11] In the instant case parties agreed that the applicant would accept the subjects in their present condition and not be obliged to maintain them in any better condition. The lease contains no reference to putting the premises into any particular state nor any express reference to the need to repair, renew or replace any aspect of the premises. While the clause makes reference to there being the obligation on the tenants to maintain the premises wind and watertight and the upholding of the water supply and drainage both within and without the premises to the reasonable satisfaction of the landlord, that added clarification to the obligation comes before, and is subject to, the proviso that the tenant will not be obliged to maintain the premises in any better condition than they are at the date hereof, as evidenced by the Schedule of Condition. The fact that the Schedule of Condition cannot presently be located does not alter the correct interpretation of the clause. The standard to which the applicant requires to maintain the subjects is the state they were in at the time the lease was entered into.

Submissions for the respondent

[12] Counsel adopted his note of argument. The tenant’s repairing obligation is an objective one: “good and tenantable order and condition”. On a proper construction of Clause (THIRD) and in the absence of a schedule of condition, the purported exception in Clause 3 (“… provided however that the Tenants will not be obliged … to be agreed by the Parties …”) has no effect. The parties prepared a scheme which created the possibility that the tenant might be able to qualify the extent of its repairing obligation but only in circumstances where they had agreedor had an arbitrator impose upon them a Schedule of Condition. No such schedule was ever agreed and no arbitration ever took place to procure one. The necessary ingredients required to invoke the operation of the exception are absent. If the tenant had wanted to secure the protection of the possible exception which appears in Clause 3 then it was incumbent upon the tenant to secure the agreement of a Schedule of Condition or otherwise refer a suitable question to arbitration in 1984. This was not done. Accordingly, all that remains is the objective standard imposed by Clause (THIRD).

Decision

[13] Although there are obvious similarities, the provision under consideration in Dem‑Master differs from the provision in the instant case. The provision in Dem‑Master proceeds on the basis that a photographic schedule had already been prepared and was annexed to the lease. In the instant case, the preparation of the Schedule of Condition is anticipated as being a future event (albeit one that the tenant would have been well advised to bring about expeditiously). The lease expressly provides for the possibility the parties may not be able to agree it by means of the arbitration provision.

[14] The binary distinction founded on by the applicant between an obligation to put premises into repair and an obligation to keep premises in repair does not arise in the context of Clause (THIRD). Rather, there is a primary obligation and a qualification thereto, which requires the applicant to be able to point to a Schedule of Condition for it to be founded on. We consider the correct analysis of Clause (THIRD) to be as follows:

The applicant is required “to uphold, maintain and keep the premises in good and tenantable order and condition”(the “primary obligation”).
The primary obligation is given content and specificity by the inclusion of the words:
“which obligation shall include the maintenance of the premises wind and watertight and the upholding of the water supply and drainage both within and without the premises all to the reasonable satisfaction of the Landlord”.
That clause is not here significant.

The inclusion of the phrase “The Tenants hereby accept the premises in their present condition as suitable for the purpose for which they are let” precludes the tenant from contending at the outset of the lease that the premises are not in a condition which is suitable for the purpose for which they are let. That phrase does not, however, of itself affect the standard to which the tenant must maintain the premises. That is dealt with by the qualification discussed next.
The primary obligation is qualified by the inclusion of the following phrase:
“provided however that the Tenants [Applicant] will not be obliged to maintain the premises in any better condition than they are at the date hereof, as such condition shall be evidenced by a Schedule of Condition in respect of the premises to be agreed by the parties or, failing agreement, to be settled by arbitration in terms of Clause THIRTY FIRST hereof …”(the “qualification”).

The qualification to the primary obligation exists for the benefit of the tenant. It ensures that in discharging the primary obligation, the tenant is not required to put the subjects into a better condition than they were as at the date of the agreement of the lease.
However, for the qualification to be founded on by the tenant, there requires to be a Schedule of Condition (“as such condition shall be evidenced”). The preparation of a Schedule of Condition is, in effect, a condition precedent for the operation of the qualification.
Clause (THIRD) anticipates the Schedule of Condition being agreed by parties at some date after the date the lease was entered into (“shall be evidenced … to be agreed by parties”).
Clause (THIRD) sensibly makes provision for the possibility that agreement in respect of the Schedule of Condition might not be reached: (“or, failing agreement, to be settled by arbitration in terms of Clause THIRTY FIRST hereof”).
It appears no Schedule of Condition existed when the lease was entered into (and senior counsel for the applicant candidly conceded that the applicant is currently unable to point to the existence of any such document).
It follows that the applicant may not currently found on the qualification.
In the absence of a Schedule of Condition, the qualification is not engaged. Proof of the condition of the premises by reference to extraneous circumstances is not permissible. The primary obligation – a customary, objective standard for a repairing obligation - remains unqualified.
The aforementioned arbitration provision relates to the settling of the document which is the Schedule of Condition. It may not be relied upon decades later to provide a retrospective assessment of the condition of the property in 1984 other than by the settling of the Schedule of Condition.
It may or may not be (and, quantum valeat , we very strongly suspect it is) impracticable to now have the Schedule of Condition settled by arbitration. However, just as the omission of the preparation of the expected photographic schedule could not affect the determination of the proper construction of the lease in Dem‑Master , in the instant case neither can either the absence of the Schedule of Condition or the fact (if indeed it be a fact) that it is not now possible to obtain a Schedule of Condition affect the proper construction of the lease.

[15] This analysis is, we consider, consistent with the principles of contractual construction narrated above. It is consistent with the natural and ordinary meaning of the words used. The requirement for a Schedule of Condition in order for the qualification to the primary obligation to be engaged results in the different components of Clause (THIRD) complementing rather than contradicting one another. We do not think it would be consistent with commercial common sense for parties to have agreed that they would be entitled at the ish in the 22 nd Century to embark upon enquiry as to the condition of the premises in 1984 by reference to extrinsic evidence: that is presumably precisely why provision is made in the lease for a Schedule of Condition which, had it been procured, would itself document an objective standard of repair.

[16] We shall fix a procedural hearing at which further procedure can be determined in light of this opinion. All questions of expenses are reserved.

for the respondent: Mr S Manson, advocate, instructed by Dentons UK and Middle East LLP
